title: What Does the CEO of a $30M ARR Startup Actually Do?
normalization: Concatenate utf8 segments per caption event; retain event start and duration; whitespace trim only.

segments.text: I run two bootstrap SaaS companies,
Orbity and retention.com, that do over
30 million a year in combined revenue.
But my daily routine might surprise you.
I drop my daughter off at preschool on
an e-bike at 8:15 every morning. I get
to the office at 8:30. I leave at 5:30,
and I don't work outside of those hours,
and I don't work weekends. Most people
who run a 30 million ARR business would
probably look at my calendar and say
it's a joke, that I'm not grinding hard
enough, that I'm not hustling enough,
and that I'm not ambitious enough. And
maybe they're right, but I've been doing
this for 11 years now, and it has worked
out fairly well. So, in this video, I'm
going to walk through my entire week day
by day, explain why I run things like
this, because I believe how most CEOs
spend their time is [music] completely
broken. Now, Monday's my internal
meeting day. Monday is the one day per
week where I batch all my internal
meetings. I do one-on-ones with Rob,
Tate, Kelly, and Diana, my direct
reports. Then we have a 90-minute L10
with the executive team, followed by a
60-minute L10 with my Orbity team. We
run EOS at our company, which is the
Entrepreneurial Operating System by Gino
Wickman, and an L10 is a specific
meeting format that comes with that
framework. The structure of the meeting
starts off with each person going over
what's called their rocks, or what they
committed to for the quarter. We then go
through our scorecard, which tracks key
metrics and how we're doing against our
annual goals. We go over our to-do's,
which is what we said that we would do
the week before, and whether or not that
got done. We then go into issue
processing. Things we need to discuss
with everybody on that meeting. Any
issues that don't need everybody in that
meeting get discussed elsewhere. And
most importantly, our executive coach,
Jonathan Shapiro, moderates the meeting
every week. Why? He does it so that we
stay on track. It's way too easy to
start processing issues and trying to
solve problems when you're going over
the scorecard or going over your rocks.
The reason why I batch all of this in
one day is because I learned the hard
way what happens if you don't. Back in
2022, I hired 50 people in under 60 days
at retention.com. We were doing 12
million ARR with just six people and I
thought that we had a unicorn, so I
tried to scale fast. It was the worst
decision I ever made as an entrepreneur.
Once we had all those people, one full
day per week became internal meetings
just to understand what everybody was
doing. One or two more days were
interviews and meetings with investors
to try to figure out if I wanted to
raise money while I kept growing head
count. I was only spending two days a
week actually selling working on product
and creating awareness. As the person
who is best at improving the product and
go-to-market, I was wasting 60% of my
time not doing these things. Things that
took two hours with two people started
taking two weeks. So now, by cramming
every internal meeting into Monday, I
protect the rest of the week for work
that actually grows my business. My
latest SaaS, ARBDDB, hit 7 million ARR
with a small and efficient team that
only works if I'm spending time in the
product and customers and not managing
meetings all week. Tuesday for me is my
content day. Tuesdays entirely dedicated
to making content. I do a one-hour live
session every week called Unfuck My
Startup. It's workshop-style content
that helps early-stage founders grow
their startup. I try to write three
LinkedIn posts. Though I'll be honest, I
usually don't get all three done on
Tuesday. And I record one YouTube video
like this one you're watching right now.
I do a one-hour LinkedIn idea meeting
with Alec, who is my LinkedIn
consultant. We mainly talk through
ideas, what's going on in my life, what
worked last week, what to write next
week. And we try to have a hook and
three bullets fleshed out for up to five
posts for the next week, so I can sit
down and just start writing. And really
importantly, if we can't come up with a
hook, the post doesn't get written, full
stop. The hook is everything. I do a
30-minute session with my Twitter
ghostwriters. This is interview format
where they ask me seven questions. A
couple of those questions are always
snipes, which is commentary about
another super viral and relevant tweet
that happened in the prior [music] week.
This is not a random choice to dedicate
an entire day to content. Content is the
growth engine behind my companies, and
I've gotten 16 million LinkedIn
impressions over the past 12 months.
That drives 30,000 unique visitors per
month to RBDB's website and is the main
driver of our sign-up. The reason I
protect a full day for this is the same
reason I batch meetings on Monday.
Writing good posts takes deep focus.
Recording a YouTube video takes deep
focus. You can't do either of these
things well if you're jumping in and out
of Slack or hopping on a call every
hour. And by the way, if you're running
a SaaS and you want to know exactly
who's visiting your website at the
person level, not just the company, then
check out what we built at RBDB by
clicking the first link in the
descriptions. It's completely free to
start using it. Now, back to the video.
Wednesday is customer call day.
Wednesday afternoon from 1:00 to 4:00
p.m. Central, I do back-to-back
15-minute customer calls. This is about
40 calls per month, which covers roughly
15% of our paying customers. The morning
is dedicated to marketing outside of
creating content for both retention.com
and RBDB. This is like whatever, ad
strategies, cold email, website copy
updates, or whatever else we have going
on. And this is something I'll never
stop doing, no matter how big the
company gets. Those calls are how I
figure out what people are upset about,
what we need to build, and where we're
going with RBDB. When I had 50 people at
retention.com, I was so far removed from
the customer that I couldn't distinguish
signal from noise. Now, I hear directly
every single week. easy for a CEO at
this revenue level to stop talking to
customers entirely. They've got VPs and
directors and managers who filter out
everything before it reaches them. But
that filtering is exactly what makes you
slow and disconnected. I'd rather spend
3 hours on a Wednesday afternoon hearing
it firsthand than spend a whole quarter
building the wrong thing because someone
three levels down misinterpreted the
feedback. The other thing I do on
Wednesdays is marketing for both
businesses outside of content. We do
cold email, we do ads, we're always
making landing pages, we're making copy
changes to the website. We do a 1-hour
call with the marketing team and go over
whatever we were working on the prior
week. Thursdays and Fridays I keep
intentionally unstructured. This is
where I catch up on LinkedIn posts that
I didn't get done on Tuesday. I work on
product or any to-dos that came out of
the marketing call I did on Wednesday. I
take calls with Rob and Tate about
reinventing our B2B. Tate and Rob are
the two people that are working
full-time in that company with me. I
also talk to super smart people about
content and virality trying to see what
I can learn from them or I talk to
industry people trying to figure out
stuff so that we can share ideas with
each other and get better. I also work
on crazy experiments that I'm running
that quarter, most of which fail. For
example, last year in the fourth quarter
I tried to create four courses and a
community then bundle all that with our
B2B SaaS product to sell in an annual
deal in a one-to-many format. I saw
Russell Brunson do this with prolific
success with ClickFunnels. It was an
enormous amount of time, money, and
energy and it didn't work for me. So, I
pulled the plug. I also go to one YPO
forum meeting per month which takes a
full Thursday. YPO is a CEO group of
people with over 20 million in revenue.
It's like structured group therapy. You
meet once a month in person with eight
to 10 people and it becomes a big part
of your life. I also do a bi-weekly
one-on-one meeting with my executive
coach Jonathan Shapiro. We talk about
any issues I'm having with the business
and are constantly working on improving
my communication. We do quarterly
executive offsites that require a little
bit of travel, but other than that, I
don't travel much. These whatever days
are also when I love meeting people in
the morning for sauna cold plunges. I
prefer sauna cold plunge to coffee,
lunch, or beer and I usually meet people
who are doing similar things to me in
similar markets. We talk about our
company, our life, our families, our
pets, whatever's is on and I love the
sauna cold plunge meeting because you
leave feeling amazing and you usually
have a great day. The reason these days
are unstructured is because that's where
the best stuff happens. The experiments,
the random conversation, these are the
ideas that turn into the [music] next
feature or growth channel. If every
single hour of your week is spoken for,
you never have time to think and
thinking time is the most valuable thing
a CEO has. So, why does this work for me
long-term? Now, I said at the top that
most eight-figure CEOs would look at
this and say it's a joke that I'm not
grinding enough, that I'm not hustling
enough, that I'm not trying hard enough,
or that I'm not ambitious enough. And
maybe that's true, but here's how I see
it. I've been in this game in one way or
another for 11 years. I built and exited
Robly email marketing, then I
bootstrapped retention.com to over 20
million AR, and now I built ARB to B.
When I look at this calendar, my honest
thought is I could do this for another
30 years. And if I do this for another
30 years, this thing will be a colossal
success. That's the part that most
founders don't think about. They
optimize for maximum intensity right now
and burn out in three to five years. I'd
rather go to pace I can sustain for
decades. Smaller teams that are
laser-focused on a few things get far
more done, move way faster, and the
founders can have better work-life
balance. That's not a trade-off, those
things go together. Fewer people means
fewer fire drills, fewer internal
meetings, fewer people problems, and it
means you spend your time on product and
your customers instead of on managing
managers. So, if you're a founder and
you feel like you need to grind 80 hours
a week to be taken seriously, I'd push
back on that. The question isn't how
many hours you're working, it's whether
you're spending those hours on things
that actually matter. Now, if you want
